title: What is known about 1RB0LD_1RC0RF_0LD0LE_1RF1LC_0LB1LE_0RA---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LD_1RC0RF_0LD0LE_1RF1LC_0LB1LE_0RA---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The tape is a list of blocks (010)^n separated by short walls (10)^s (s = 4, 5, 6 or 8) and, near the right end, by single 1s. Each time the head comes back to the left end in state C, the first block has lost 4 copies and the i-th block 3·4i−1 copies: a counter in base 4 whose digits are whole blocks. When the first block is down to 5 copies, a wall phase of s−1 visits eats 3 copies per visit from the second block, which then becomes the new first block (seen: 48 → 17; predicted next: 792 → 773). The tail at the right end runs a cycle of four visits that adds one block of 4k-sized length. Shift rules are proved in Lean; the list rule is checked against the run. The halting condition at the level of the list is not identified yet.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 67,112 cells have been visited and 22,378 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.051). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.483).

claims.title: Shift rules over the (010) background
claims.text: Eight shift rules for every length n, among them the wall 1011 crossing (010)^2n to the right in 28n steps, the turn at the right end (38n+20 steps), and the left-going crossings of (010), (001), (100) in 5n steps.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>11</sup> steps
claims.text: A plain C simulator (longrun.c, on tools/c/tm.h) runs 1011 steps from blank tape without a halt; at the end the head has visited cells -122 to 896,652 and 298,934 cells hold a 1.

claims.title: No halt in the first 3.83×10<sup>19</sup> steps (exact macro run)
claims.text: A macro simulator (blocks of 6 cells, long runs of equal blocks crossed in one go; exact: every macro step is a run of the machine, counted step for step) ran from blank tape to step 38,350,288,749,170,965,057 without a halt. At this block size it gives the same state, head position and tape as the direct simulator after 2,000,061,359 steps. This is a bounded run and says nothing about later steps.

claims.title: The list at the left-end visits
claims.text: All 51 visits of the head to the left end in state C up to 1.54·1010 steps were read off the direct run. Between consecutive visits of the main phase the first block loses 4 copies and block i loses 3·4i−1 (every comparison agrees); a wall phase (96, 93, 90) reloads the first block with 89, which runs 89, 85, …, 5; a second wall phase (36, 33, …, 18) reloads it with 17, which runs 17, 13, 9, 5.

claims.title: A deterministic counter, no sign of a halt
claims.text: The run is a nested counter whose digits are block lengths of the form 3·4<sup>k</sup>m (plus 1 at the tail); nothing random is involved, so the probviously argument does not apply. Halting needs F to read 1; hand-made tapes with other walls in front of the second block (s = 6 instead of 4 or 8) also ran 1.5·10<sup>10</sup> steps without a halt.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The list rule is deterministic but has more cases than are written down here (a second form with (001)^n blocks, the walls of 5 and 6 near the tail); the halting condition at the level of the list is not identified.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. This machine is a counter in base 4 whose digits are whole blocks of the tape: each time the head comes back to the left end, the first block loses 4 copies, the second 12, the third 48, and so on; when the first block runs out, the second one takes its place.

facts.text: How the head crosses the (010) background, proved for every length.
Copies lost per visit by the first, second, third block.
No halt in the C simulator.

sections.heading: A counter whose digits are blocks
html: Look at the tape each time the head is back at the left end in state C. It reads (010)^a1 (10)^s1 (010)^a2 (10)^s2 …: blocks of 010 separated by short walls. One visit to the next:

So the wall in front of block i drifts four times slower than the one before it, which is what the picture shows. A block that reaches zero disappears and its two walls merge ((10)^4 and (10)^4 give (10)^8).

When the first block is down to 5, a wall phase starts: for s−1 visits the second block loses 3 copies per visit while the wall in front of it wears down, and then that block (less one copy) becomes the new first block. In the run this happened with 48 → 17 (new first block = old second − 3s − 7), and the same rule predicts 792 → 773 next; both are 1 more than a multiple of 4, which the main phase needs to land on 5 again.
At the right end the last block, separated by single 1s, goes through a cycle of four visits that ends with a new block 32 times the rate of the old last one, so the list keeps growing.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.051). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.483).
After 109 steps the tape spans 67,112 cells (68 left of the start, 53,450 right), with a density of 1s of 0.333.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machines below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in any of the others, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

family: Base-4 drifting counter: blocks of (010)^n eaten at rates 4, 12, 48, 192, ... with a wall phase that reloads the first block
summary: A nested counter on blocks of (010)^n: at every visit of the head to the left end the first block loses 4 copies and the i-th loses 3*4^(i-1); when the first runs out, a wall phase turns the second block into the new first one, and a period-4 cycle at the right end keeps adding blocks.
